---
title: Mapping data to space
format: gfm
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(ggplot2) 
library(dplyr)
library(sf)
```

## Choropleths

Let's make a choropleth! Pick any of the tract-level data we have available in justviz (ACS [`acs`], CDC [`cdc`], EJSCREEN [`ej_natl`], vacants [`vacants_by_tract`], or climate vulnerability [`climate`]), reshape or filter it if necessary to have your variable of interest as its own column (i.e. CDC needs to be reshaped to wide format or filtered for just one indicator). Join it with a tract shapefile (`justviz::tracts_sf`, get a full set of the state's tracts with `tigris::tracts`, and/or filter for whatever counties you want), making sure to put the `sf` data frame on the left side of your join so you retain its data type. Then use `geom_sf` to make a choropleth of a continuous variable. Use `scale_fill_distiller` to use a ColorBrewer palette on continuous data.

```{r}
#| label: choro-distiller 

# load climate data and picked tree canopy cover as variable of interest
clim <- justviz::climate |>
  select(geoid, tcc)

# i wanna look at all of maryland --> load from tigris
md_tracts <- tigris::tracts(state = "MD", cb = TRUE, year = 2020)

clim_sf <- md_tracts |>
  left_join(clim, by = c("GEOID" = "geoid"))

ggplot(clim_sf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = tcc, color = "Census tract"), linewidth = 0.01) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Greens",
                       direction = 1,
                       labels = scales::label_percent()) + 
  # legend hacking to show census tract border
  # (using black or white is ugly across whole state, but darkgreen pretty but
  # could be misinterpreted as lines of 100% canopy cover)
  scale_color_manual(values = "darkgreen", name = NULL) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5))) +  
  labs(title = "Tree canopy cover by census tract in Maryland",
       fill = "Tree canopy cover") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Study the docs for `scale_fill_distiller` to understand the difference between the brewer, distiller, and fermenter variants (beyond the punny names). Try all three with your data---only 2 of them will work. Decide which you like best for this data. What tradeoffs do you find between legibility and precision?

```{r}
#| label: choro-more-scales 
#| error: true

testing_palettes <-
  ggplot(clim_sf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = tcc, color = "Census tract"), linewidth = 0.01) +
  scale_color_manual(values = "darkgreen", name = NULL) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5))) 

# distiller
testing_palettes +
   scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Greens",
                        direction = 1,
                        labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(title = "Tree canopy cover by census tract in Maryland, scale_fill_distiller",
       fill = "Tree canopy cover") 

#fermenter
testing_palettes + 
  scale_fill_fermenter(palette = "Greens",
                       direction = 1,
                      labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(title = "Tree canopy cover by census tract in Maryland, scale_fill_fermenter",
       fill = "Tree canopy cover") 

# brewer
testing_palettes +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Greens",
                    direction = 1,
                    labels = scales::label_percent()) + # this one doesnt work
  labs(title = "Tree canopy cover by census tract in Maryland, scale_fill_brewer",
       fill = "Tree canopy cover") 
```
Originally, I used distiller because that's what the course notes has as an example. I still like distiller better than the other two. It doesn't bin together data like fermenter does, and brewer doesn't work b/c it's meant for discrete data, not continuous. I like how the map shows the full range of the data, even if some values may not be as easy to tell apart. Fermenter loses precision in favor of legibility.

## Binning algorithms

It's common to use binning algorithms to cut continuous values into bins for a choropleth, but the choice of algorithm can dramatically change how the data is understood. The function `justviz::jenks` will cut a continuous variable into binned values and return a factor, using the Jenks/Fisher algorithms. These are designed to highlight skewed data well, but aren't the best choice for all situations.

Instead, experiment with the function `classInt::classify_intervals`, which gives you access to several different algorithms. Depending on the algorithm and distribution of your data, the number of classes you request might be a goal but not necessarily what you get. Use it like this:

```{r}
#| label: classint
#| eval: false 
justviz::ej_natl |>
    dplyr::filter(indicator == "pm25") |>
    dplyr::mutate(value_brk = classInt::classify_intervals(value_ptile, n = 5, style = "pretty"))
```

Now before remaking your choropleth, cut the variable into bins using one of the algorithms available in `classify_intervals` (look at the function docs). The binned column will be a factor. Use this column for the choropleth's fill, and use the same palette as above with `scale_fill_brewer`. Try multiple algorithms---some will give you way more bins than you can get a palette for, some will give too few to be useful, so just mess around with arguments.

```{r}
#| label: choro-binned

# how many bins/whats the dist for each?
  tcc_equal    = classInt::classify_intervals(clim_sf$tcc, n = 5, style = "equal")
  tcc_quantile = classInt::classify_intervals(clim_sf$tcc, n = 5, style = "quantile")
  tcc_fisher   = classInt::classify_intervals(clim_sf$tcc, n = 5, style = "fisher")
  tcc_pretty   = classInt::classify_intervals(clim_sf$tcc, n = 5, style = "pretty")
  tcc_sd       = classInt::classify_intervals(clim_sf$tcc, style = "sd")

# print
  table(tcc_equal)
  table(tcc_quantile)
  table(tcc_fisher)
  table(tcc_pretty)
  table(tcc_sd)
  
# add each binning to clim_sf
  clim_sf <- clim_sf |>
    mutate(
      tcc_equal    = classInt::classify_intervals(tcc, n = 5, style = "equal"),
      tcc_quantile = classInt::classify_intervals(tcc, n = 5, style = "quantile"),
      tcc_fisher   = classInt::classify_intervals(tcc, n = 5, style = "fisher"),
      tcc_pretty = classInt::classify_intervals(tcc, n = 5, style = "pretty"),
      tcc_sd = classInt::classify_intervals(tcc, style = "sd")
  )
  
# so I can copy paste with diff binning algorithms  
binning_base <- ggplot(clim_sf) +
  scale_color_manual(values = "darkgreen", name = NULL) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5))) +
  theme_minimal()


# two different binning algorithms:
# fisher
binning_base +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = tcc_fisher, color = "Census tract"), linewidth = 0.01) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Greens", direction = 1, na.value = "grey80") +
  labs(title = "Tree canopy cover by census tract in Maryland (Fisher breaks)",
       fill = "Tree canopy cover")
# quantile
binning_base +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = tcc_quantile, color = "Census tract"), linewidth = 0.01) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Greens", direction = 1, na.value = "grey80") +
  labs(title = "Tree canopy cover by census tract in Maryland (quantile breaks)",
       fill = "Tree canopy cover")
```

## Do it all again

Now that you've made a choropleth with a sequential fill, and found a binning algorithm that works well for the same data, try it all again with a different variable. Pick something with a different distribution---if the first variable was very skewed, try something closer to a normal or uniform distribution.

```{r}
#| label: chloro-cdc

cdc <- justviz::cdc |>
  filter(indicator == "Annual checkup") |>  
  select(location, value)

cdc_sf <- md_tracts |>
  left_join(cdc, by = c("GEOID" = "location"))

# how many bins/whats the dist for each?
  cdc_equal    = classInt::classify_intervals(cdc_sf$value, n = 5, style = "equal")
  cdc_quantile = classInt::classify_intervals(cdc_sf$value, n = 5, style = "quantile")
  cdc_fisher   = classInt::classify_intervals(cdc_sf$value, n = 5, style = "fisher")
  cdc_pretty   = classInt::classify_intervals(cdc_sf$value, n = 5, style = "pretty")
  cdc_sd       = classInt::classify_intervals(cdc_sf$value, style = "sd")
  
cdc_sf <- cdc_sf |>
mutate(value_brk = classInt::classify_intervals(value, n = 5, style = "fisher"))

# continuous
ggplot(cdc_sf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = value, color = "Census tract"), linewidth = 0.01) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Blues", direction = 1, na.value = "grey80") +
  scale_color_manual(values = "#08306B", name = NULL) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5))) +
  labs(title = "Adults who got an annual checkup by census tract in Maryland",
       fill = "Annual checkup (%)") +
  theme_minimal()

# binned
ggplot(cdc_sf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = value_brk, color = "Census tract"), linewidth = 0.01) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues", direction = 1, na.value = "grey80") +
  scale_color_manual(values = "#08519C", name = NULL) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5))) +
  labs(title = "Adults who got an annual checkup by census tract in Maryland (Fisher breaks)",
       fill = "Annual checkup (%)") +
  theme_minimal()

```
